author: nero_eth
content:
Am I understanding the current specs around IL equivocation correctly and ever includer can basically send out 2 ILs.

Since equivocations are not proven by the next proposer by putting them into the block, the safest strategy for the proposer is to include the txs of both ILs - and there is no punishment for equivocating.
Is this intended? We're allowing 2x the actually needed networking traffic (=peers must forward 2 ILs per includer).

I'd prefer only ever forwarding 1 IL per peer and instead put equivocations into the block (2x transactions_root + 2x signature) + a gossip topic for forwarding the equivocation proof.

author: nero_eth
content:
It's not only broadcasting 2x but also 2x more work for builders in the worst-case. 
With frame txs, builders will have to include the tx_index where they tried inserting the transaction. 
Under asynchrony, builders may want to obey both ILs and they could have different txs (both ILs containing txs maxxing-out the VERIFY gas from eip-8141). This doubles work.

author: nero_eth
content:
And there could even be weird interactions with the transactions of equivocating ILs, which might be hard to test.
My feeling is we should include the proofs in the block, have a gossip topic for forwarding equivocation proofs, and ignore every IL from an includer from whom we've already seen one and instead create an equivocation proof.
Post-pq we can either aggregate the proof into the block's proof, or just keep including them in the block (which seems fine to).

author: jih2nn
content:
I think there are multiple ways to resolve this concern.

1) Make a bid includes a list of IL roots, instead of an IL bitlist, which is an idea brought up here: https://discord.com/channels/595666850260713488/1210529202458071050/1567124235233656934. An attester can tell whether there was an equivocation when a bid has a different IL root than what it has for the same includer. With this approach, we can broadcast only one IL per includer, but equivocating ILs are enforced with the one that a builder chooses.

However, I think it should be IL transactions roots and aggregated IL signatures. An attester will compute IL root and verify it against the aggregated signature. This is to prevent any forgery by builders. This aggregation should be benchmarked especially post-PQ. (cc <@1035747431461167125> for the IL roots in a bid design.)

2) Add an equivocation proof to the envelope. A naive approach is making a proof of two `SignedInclusionListHeader`. The proof varies depending on the design, e.g. aggregated signature.

```
class InclusionListHeader(Container):
    slot: Slot
    validator_index: ValidatorIndex
    dependent_root: Root
    transactions_root: Root

class SignedInclusionListHeader(Container):
    message: InclusionListHeader
    signature: BLSSignature # leanXMSS signature post-PQ

class InclusionListEquivocation(Container):
    signed_header_1: SignedInclusionListHeader
    signed_header_2: SignedInclusionListHeader
```

There maybe more options with different trade-offs.

author: jih2nn
content:
> have a gossip topic for forwarding equivocation proofs, and ignore every IL from an includer from whom we've already seen one and instead create an equivocation proof.

While this would reduce the bandwidth consumption when there is any equivocation, it requires a careful examination on whether there will be any edge cases caused by the new gossip topic. Maybe it's worth to explore post-PQ but it also depends on the performance of our future p2p layer.
